children: The US generated 1.29 billion ethanol (D6) blending credits in August, about the same as in July, according to Environmental Protection Agency data released on Thursday.
Bio-based diesel blending credits (D4) fell to 693 million, from 796 million in July, the data showed.

The credits, known as Renewable Identification Numbers (RINs), are used by refiners to comply with the Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS), which requires renewable fuels such as ethanol and bio-based diesel to be blended into the fuel supply. Every gallon of biofuel produced generates RINs, and those who do not generate enough credits must buy them in the open market.

D4 and D6 RIN prices surged to record highs this year after the EPA finalized its most aggressive renewable fuel blending mandates for 2026 and 2027. While prices have eased from those peaks following the agency's approval of widespread small-refinery waivers, they remain well above historical levels.a
End-of-day values for D4 credits were $2.05 each, while D6 RIN prices landed at $2.00 each, up slightly from Wednesday, according to Argus Media.

Lower generation of biodiesel and renewable diesel credits in August was partly driven by rising exports, as tight global diesel supplies prompted overseas buyers to pay high premiums for renewable diesel, said Paul Winters, director of public affairs and federal communications at the Clean Fuels Alliance America.

"RIN retirements for exports have picked up over the last two months," he said, noting that 547 million D4 RINs had been retired for exports by the end of August, compared with 379 million during the first six months of the year.
RINs generated from renewable diesel destined for export must be retired and cannot be used to meet US renewable fuel compliance obligations.
